items.quote: How, and with what Vertue, Physick worketh upon Mans body and cureth his Diseases
items.note: The chapter is headed and numbered as one subject: how and by what virtue physic works on the body and cures.

items.name: Hippocrates
items.quote: according to Hippocrates his Maxim, that Contraryes are to be cured with CONTRARYES
items.note: The maxim that contraries cure contraries is given to Hippocrates.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: or Like with LIKE, according to Paracelsus
items.note: The opposing maxim, like with like, is given to Paracelsus; the paragraph frames the two as what physicians dispute.

items.name: lib. de flatibus
items.quote: In lib. de flatibus.
items.note: A margin note names a writing beside the Hippocratic maxim, as the place the words come from.

items.quote: these Maxims may be both received in the Anatomy of Nature, though they seem thwart one the other
items.note: The author holds that both maxims can be accepted; their disagreement is only apparent.

items.quote: because they cannot understand how to reconcile them by a seasonable and sutable interpretation
items.note: Philosophers seem at variance only to readers who cannot interpret them suitably; the author asks for reconciling interpretation.

items.quote: For Physick is nothing else but an opposition of those things that are desired, to wit, a refreshing of the strength and Balsom, and a removing of superfluityes or impurities that cause diseases
items.note: The text says what physic is: restoring strength and Balsom, and removing impurities.

items.name: Hippocrates
items.quote: that hunger is to to be cured with meat, thirst with drink, fulnesse with evacuation
items.note: Hippocrates' contraries are given as hunger cured by meat, thirst by drink and the like; Paracelsus is said not to fault him for this.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Paracelsus therefore doth not find fault with Hippocrates
items.note: Paracelsus is reported as accepting Hippocrates' contraries in this sense.

items.name: Galen
items.quote: But he is poynt blanck against Galen, who applyed that Contrariety of Hippocrates chiefly to those bare and naked qualityes which Hippocrates utterly disclaimed
items.note: Galen is reported as applying the contrariety to bare qualities; Paracelsus is said to oppose him.

items.name: Galen
items.quote: referred the first and principall Idaea's of Cures to Refrigerations, Calefactions, Humectations, Exsiccations
items.note: Galen's view, rejected as an unhappy mistake: cures rest on cooling, heating, moistening, drying.

items.quote: The onely and alone NATURES of Physicall medicines, as hath been said, or those Hippocraticall vertues are they which doe the cures
items.note: Points back to an earlier place where the natures of medicines were said to cure.

items.quote: the Physitian is but the minister or servant
items.note: The physician only serves; the natures of medicines do the cure.

items.quote: this very selfe same Nature, which is our Life and Balsom, or balsomicall Mummy, that preserveth the body from all corruption
items.note: Nature is equated with our life, Balsom and balsamic Mummy, which keeps the body from corruption.

items.quote: by means of the Saline moysture, that is, of the inferiour Balsom springing up in the inferiour from the superiour
items.note: The Saline moisture is said to be the inferior Balsom, springing up in the inferior from the superior.

items.quote: sometimes worketh wonders, when the Physitians to their great disgrace and shame of their Profession could doe no good
items.note: Nature heals where physicians fail and have given the patient up.

items.quote: is its own proper Physitian in Mans body, who asketh nothing of the outward Physitian but Instauration
items.note: Our Nature is its own physician; the outward physician only supplies Instauration.

items.quote: Instauration, or as tis commonly called, fortification applyed to the diseased part by a most pure medicine when the like Nature is not at hand
items.note: Instauration is glossed as fortification of the diseased part by a pure medicine.

items.quote: the Medicinall Balsom like a coadjutour or privy counsellour assisteth the Vitall or Radicall and Naturall Balsom because of the simpathy and common agreement between them
items.note: The medicine's Balsom helps the body's own Balsom through sympathy between like things.

items.quote: as an inward and unknown Antidote to chase all its enemies out of its Monarchy by the onely power of the Vitall facultyes
items.note: Restored Nature is figured as an unknown inward antidote ruling a monarchy; figurative wording for the body's own healing.

items.quote: Nature cureth with like things.
items.note: The margin sums the paragraph as cure by like things.

items.quote: To go about to cure a disease with contrary qualities, is to raise and stir up intrinsick commotions to the utter overthrow of Nature
items.note: Cure by contrary qualities harms an already weakened Nature.

items.quote: where there is no true action and passion, there can follow no true Naturall effect
items.note: Contraries do not act on each other, so they yield no natural effect.

items.quote: medicines should not be contrary to the grieved part, but very agreeable to it
items.note: Medicines must agree with the affected part, sharing its nature outwardly as the part has it inwardly.

items.quote: Man is therefore called a Microcosm or little world, because the whole world preserveth, nourisheth and cureth him
items.note: The text gives the reason man is called Microcosm.

items.quote: When the fruits of the Earth, Aire, Water and Fire of the Microcosm are sick, they must be restored by fruits like themselves of the Macrocosm
items.note: The four elements in man are restored by their likes in the great world.

items.quote: every Nature is Naturally the best preserver of it selfe
items.note: Nature helped by its own nature drives out enemies.

items.name: Galen
items.quote: it alone being the genuine Physitian of all diseases, as Galen witnesseth in his 13 Book of Method
items.note: Galen is cited as witness that Nature alone is the physician of diseases, though CH4.2 sets Paracelsus against him.

items.quote: It is the First Mover of every cure
items.what: the First Mover of every cure
items.note: Nature is named the first mover of every cure; without it all physic is vain.

items.quote: it selfe healeth its own infirmities by the innate Mummy
items.note: Nature heals by the innate Mummy; without the inward Nature diseases prove mortal.

items.quote: those that are wounded perceive a presentaneous succour from Nature as of one hastening to helpe
items.note: Experience of wounds is offered as proof that Nature hastens to heal and preserve itself.

items.quote: they are not much mistaken if they have not respect to the qulaityes, but the vertues of a contrary Nature
items.note: Cure by contraries is allowed if it means contrary virtues, not contrary qualities.

items.quote: For there are as many crosse and hurtfull vertues to nature as there be good and healthfull for it
items.note: Virtues are good or hurtful; good virtues drive out hurtful ones.

items.quote: contrary qualityes, are not rooted out by contrary quallityes, but rather are irritated and provoked to strife by each other
items.note: Contrary qualities only provoke each other and weaken Nature.

items.quote: because Nature is not a quality but a vertue
items.note: The text says what Nature is: a virtue, not a quality.

items.quote: but Nature her selfe (who is the Internall Mummy or inward Balsom)
items.note: Nature is equated with the Internal Mummy or inward Balsom; she, not the physician, expels disease.

items.quote: when her own inward strength fayleth shee is to be supplyed with outward helpe by her servant the Physitian
items.note: The physician is Nature's servant, helping only when her strength fails.

items.quote: it may be the best medicine not to use any medicine at all but to leave the ooperation to the sole Archaeus or Art of Nature
items.note: Archaeus is equated with the Art of Nature; sometimes no medicine is best.

items.quote: The Inward Physitian doth the work, when the Naturall Physitian faileth.
items.note: The margin speaks of an Inward Physitian working when the Naturall Physitian fails; the paragraph elsewhere calls Nature the physician, so the note's use of Naturall for the failing physician stands apart.

items.quote: if any be preserved in a raging pestilence by Opium which is most cold, it is not by the coldnesse of Opium, but but by the Specifick venemous vertue of the Opium
items.note: Opium helps in plague by its specific poisonous virtue, not by its coldness.

items.quote: which hath a greater degree of poyson then the occult venomous power of that Pestilence
items.note: The pestilence has an occult venomous power, overcome by a stronger poison.

items.quote: Thus Nature destroyeth one poyson by another, it subdueth a weak evill by a stronger
items.note: Nature fights with hurtful as well as healthful weapons.

items.quote: As winter doth not destroy summer, nor summer winter, but one gives place to the other, so one quality doth not destroy another
items.note: Qualities do not destroy one another; the seasons are the comparison.

items.quote: for without vertue the quallity is dead and wholly accidentall
items.note: A quality without virtue gives no life or substance, which a medicine must give.

items.quote: Roots of diseases in the body of Man are neither hot nor cold
items.note: Disease roots have no heat or cold; disease is only called hot or cold.

items.quote: those Accidents and Excrements are but the signes of the disease, and not the disease it selfe
items.note: Heat, cold and excrements are signs, not the disease.

items.quote: the most pernitious diseases and Traytors of the body do not spring out of the matter of the body, or out of the four Humours
items.note: The worst diseases do not come from bodily matter or the four Humours.

items.quote: but from the Nature of the Seed or Astra's and Invisible mechanick Spirits of the Three principles
items.note: Diseases spring from the Seed, equated with Astra's and invisible mechanic Spirits of the Three principles.

items.quote: which Spirits also build their outward house and habitation with shells
items.note: The disease-spirits are pictured as builders of a shelled house; figurative wording for the visible body of a disease.

items.quote: These Forgers and Invisible Astra's of diseases were not knowne to the Ancients.
items.note: The author says the Ancients did not know these hidden causes.

items.quote: Physick is a Spirit (not a body) which the Magician or wise man only can discerne
items.note: Physic is a spirit that only the Magician or wise man can discern: knowledge limited to some.

items.quote: the body or Earth of Simples is to be cast away
items.note: In preparing simples, their body or earth is discarded.

items.quote: and the vertue Heaven or Astrum of it only to be taken
items.note: The virtue of a simple is equated with its Heaven or Astrum, the part kept.

items.quote: it is necessary that the life should worke upon the life, and the Spirit upon the Spirit by sepration of the impure body
items.note: Separation of the impure body lets spirit work on spirit, compared to the sun melting snow.

items.quote: Such is the Nature of all Secrets that they worke without the matter and body because the diseases also are not bodyes
items.note: Secrets work without matter because diseases are not bodies.

items.quote: This is the true and lively Anatomy.
items.note: The account of spirit working on spirit is named the true Anatomy.

items.quote: This Mechanick and Forger of diseases is to be subdued and destroyed in his Roote and originall
items.note: Disease must be destroyed at its root, as a tree in its seed.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Paracelsus in the Tincture of medicines.
items.note: A margin note names Paracelsus and a writing beside the passage on destroying disease at the root.

items.quote: the Mechanick Forger or principle of a Pear's generation hath his habitation in the Roote, not in the branch
items.note: Tree, pear and grass images figure the seed or root of disease.

items.quote: the grasse which groweth of its own accord is hindred from growing, not by evultion but corruption of the Earth
items.note: Growth is stopped by corrupting the ground, not by pulling up; given as a likeness for cure at the root.

items.name: great Surgery
items.quote: See the first Tract of the second book of great Surgery
items.note: A margin note sends the reader to a writing, great Surgery.

items.quote: Degrees and complexions are not considered in diseases.
items.note: The margin states that degrees and complexions do not count in diseases.

items.quote: when the Centre, Root, and Seed of diseases are pluckt up and removed the worke is done
items.note: Cure is complete when the root and seed of disease are removed.

items.quote: That Physitian which cureth by complexion is like him that would extinguish the hurtless flame and let alone the fire in the coals
items.note: Cure by complexion treats the flame and leaves the fire.

items.quote: in doing the cure the Roote of the seed which containeth the vertues is to be taken in hand
items.note: What springs from the seed is not the disease; the root of the seed is to be treated.

items.name: Book of ancient Physick
items.quote: In his Book of ancient Physick.
items.note: A margin note names a writing beside the passage.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: When Paracelsus saith that like preserve their like, and are destroyed by their contraryes, he doth not meane the first nor second qualityes
items.note: Paracelsus' saying is given, and the author says what it does not mean.

items.quote: which he alwayes calleth Recollaceous and invalid ones
items.note: Paracelsus is said to call first and second qualities Recollaceous and invalid.

items.quote: at least the Cherionic, Hippocraticall powers and vertues
items.note: Like means substance or Cherionic, Hippocratic powers; the word Cherionic is not explained here.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: the second part of his great Chyrurgye
items.note: A chapter of Paracelsus' great Chyrurgye is cited as where this sense appears.

items.quote: Like things are said to be the Remedies of diseases because they are of the same Anatomy of Nature, and because they have the like Signatures, Qualities and Roots
items.note: The text says why like things are called remedies.

items.quote: because they have the like Signatures, Qualities and Roots
items.note: Likeness in Qualities is a ground of cure here, while the same paragraph and CH4.4 deny that qualities cure and say Paracelsus does not mean qualities.

items.quote: But Contraryes cure because they piece up the defects and wants, because they appease the spirits and consentaneous impurities with a friendly saturity
items.note: The author gives the sense in which contraries do cure.

items.quote: because they attempt resolutions, consumptions and tacit ablations
items.note: Contraries are said to work by resolutions, consumptions and tacit ablations.

items.quote: Diseases are cured by applying that which is proper for them.
items.note: The margin states cure by what is proper to the disease.

items.quote: That Like are to be preferved with their Like is thus to be understood
items.note: The text says how like with like is to be understood.

items.quote: the Salt, Sulphur and Mercury of the Microcosm is preserved by the Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury of the Macrocosm analogically agreeing together
items.note: The three in man are kept by the three in the great world, by analogy.

items.quote: in the Microcosm there are various Sulphurs (one of the head, another of the heart, &c.) and various Mercuryes and Salts
items.note: Each part of man has its own Sulphur, Mercury and Salt, answered by those in herbs and minerals.

items.quote: The ministry of Fire discovereth their agreement, operation, and difference
items.note: Fire is the means of finding the agreement and difference of these substances.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: he distributeth all materiall diseases according to those three substances of which our bodies are composed
items.note: An unnamed he divides diseases by the three substances; the last person named before this, in CH4.6, is Paracelsus.

items.quote: he called them Sulphurean diseases, such are all Inflamations and Feavers
items.note: A class of disease named from kindled Sulphur.

items.quote: as Sulphur may be deprest or heightned four wayes, viz. by the four Elements
items.note: Sulphur is changed in four ways, by the four Elements.

items.quote: Those that proceed from moysture he Mercuriall.
items.note: Diseases from moisture are named Mercurial.

items.quote: Mercury may three manner of wayes be exalted above the Naturall degree
items.note: Three ways Mercury is raised: by digestive heat, by exercise, by the Astra's.

items.quote: By the heat of digestion it is distild, and so causeth all sorts of Apoplexies
items.note: Mercury distilled by digestive heat causes apoplexies.

items.quote: by the heat of Excercise it is sublimed
items.note: Mercury sublimed by exercise brings madness and frenzy.

items.quote: by the heat of the stars it is precipitated, and then causeth the Gout in hands and feet
items.note: Mercury precipitated by the stars causes gout.

items.quote: from eating and drinking those things that have too much Tattar in them
items.note: Gout is tied to food and drink with too much Tattar.

items.quote: those diseases that are bred of Salt, he calleh Saline and Nitrons
items.note: Diseases from Salt are named Saline and Nitrous.

items.quote: Salt destroyeth health 4 wayes, by Resolution, Calcination, (loosing its liquid and humid Temperament) Reverbertion. Alcalization
items.note: Four ways Salt destroys health are numbered and named.

items.quote: all which are diseases arising from the Salt dissolved
items.note: Ulcers, scabs, itch and the like come from dissolved Salt.

items.quote: Surfetting and gluttony which destroy the digestion is the cause of the Salts destruction
items.note: Excess destroys the Salt of man; the stars also move it out of its degree.

items.quote: Which Salt may be changed and turned into all sorts of Salts, and such as is the Transmutation such also is the disease
items.note: The kind of disease follows the change the Salt undergoes.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: He saith therefore that the Sulphur kindled in mans body is to be quenched with the Sulphur of the great world
items.note: He (unnamed here; Paracelsus is the last named in CH4.6) says like Sulphur quenches kindled Sulphur.

items.quote: but he that considereth to what end he spake it will find that such a remedy will be contrary to the disease
items.note: The author says the saying, read for its purpose, means a remedy contrary to the disease: the words are not to be taken at face value.

items.quote: appropriate Sulphur should be used
items.note: Kindled Sulphur from the heart is quenched with an appropriate Sulphur, such as Sulphur of Vitriol, Niter or common Salt.

items.quote: there are many to be had in Natures Garden, and the Family of Hearbs and Mineralls
items.note: Herbs and minerals are called Natures Garden and a Family.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Likewise he saith that Ulcers proceeding from Salts must be cured by Salts
items.note: He (unnamed; see CH4.6) says Salt ulcers are cured by Salts.

items.quote: but if we observe his drift, such Salts are contrary to that which was the cause of the disease
items.note: Again the author reads past the wording: the Salts meant are contrary to the cause.

items.quote: for they are incarnative and consolidative, as Frankencense, Mastick, Myrrhe, Aloes
items.note: Gums and resins are given as the Salts that cure ulcers.

items.quote: sometime he calls that Salt whatever it be that will melt, and may be resolved into a watry moysture, and then dryed and hardened by Fire
items.note: The text says what Salt sometimes means in his usage: anything that melts and hardens by fire.

items.quote: All Terresterity is the Salt of Paracelsus.
items.note: The margin equates all earthiness with Paracelsus' Salt.

items.quote: Cumfry cureth the corrosion of Salt.
items.note: Margin remedies for the three: comfrey for Salt, saffron for Sulphur, gold for Mercury.

items.quote: Gold thickneth the too much sublimation of Mercury.
items.note: Gold is named as remedy for over-sublimed Mercury.

items.quote: Our Nature cureth all diseases when he impediments are taken away
items.note: The physician's part is to remove impediments so that Nature cures.

items.quote: As there are Three from which all Physick proceedeth, Mercury, Sulphur, Salt; so likewise there are three sorts of diseases, Mercuriall, Sulphurean, Saline
items.what: Three from which all Physick proceedeth
items.note: The three principles and the three sorts of disease are set side by side.

items.quote: All Ulcers are cured by incarnating Mercury
items.note: Here all ulcers are cured by Mercury; CH4.9 says ulcers from Salts are cured by Salts.

items.quote: All mattery gluish sores by Salt
items.note: Mattery sores are cured by Salt, inflammations by Sulphur.

items.quote: This needs no Reasons to confirme it.
items.note: The author gives the scheme as needing no proof.

items.quote: Medicament though they be contrary to the disease, yet they must of necessity be altogether courteous to Nature
items.note: Medicines may oppose the disease but must be kind to Nature.

items.quote: if she sinck or miscary the Physitian can doe no good
items.note: Without Nature the physician is powerless.

items.quote: if she abide and be kept safe and sound she worketh incredible wonders
items.note: Nature kept safe works wonders; the following stories illustrate it.

items.quote: A stupendious and true Story.
items.note: The margin heads the following account as a true story.

items.quote: As was seen in the New City at Prague, Anno 1602. in a certaine rustick or countryman of Bohemia, whose name was Mathew
items.note: A dated case at Prague is given as an instance of Nature's wonders.

items.quote: by application of drawing Plaisters made of the Load-stone and other things, the poynt of the knife began to force its passage
items.note: Drawing plasters of loadstone brought the swallowed knife toward the stomach's mouth.

items.quote: it was prosperously performed by Florianis Mathis of Brandeburge chiefe Surgion of the Kingdome and City
items.note: The knife was cut out by a named surgeon.

items.quote: his stomack had changed the colour of it just as if it had laine so long in the fire
items.note: The stomach changed the knife's colour as fire would.

items.quote: as he told me
items.note: The author claims the man's own report to him.

items.name: Physitians Aphorismes
items.quote: contrary to the determinate assertion of Physitians Aphorismes
items.note: The recovery is set against what physicians' aphorisms assert.

items.quote: in the year 1606. at Prague a certaine Silesian to get mony did in the presence of many swallow six and forty white flints
items.note: A second Prague case: a man swallowed flints.

items.quote: by this bold adventure, without impairing his health, he went up and down getting his living for many years together
items.note: He lived for years without harm; the paragraph ends with &c.
